implementation_notes: The GoF structure is unnecessary here: a function-local static inside the accessor (the Meyers singleton) is initialised exactly once and thread-safely by the language since C++11, the compiler emits the guard, and destruction at program exit is defined - so no lock, no once-flag and no heap allocation are needed. The private constructor plus deleted copy/move operations still carry the uniqueness, and because the instance is created on first call, the static-initialisation-order fiasco that hits namespace-scope objects disappears. Prefer passing a reference to the instance from main or a composition root; keep the accessor for code that cannot be injected.
pitfalls: Re-entering the accessor from the constructor (the object depending on itself during initialisation) is undefined behaviour and typically deadlocks.
Destruction order across translation units is still unspecified: a static object whose destructor uses the singleton can run after the singleton has been destroyed.
The guard is per process and per shared-library copy: a plugin that statically links the class gets its own instance unless the class is exported from exactly one place.
The guarantee is only from C++11 (VS2015 on MSVC) and can be switched off (-fno-threadsafe-statics, /Zc:threadSafeInit-), which silently removes it.

variants.name: std::call_once guarded construction
variants.implementation_notes: std::call_once with a static std::once_flag gives the same once-only guarantee while keeping the constructor call explicit, and unlike a function-local static it retries after a failed attempt: if the initialiser throws, the flag is not flipped and a later call runs it again. Choose it when construction can fail, needs arguments captured at run time, or when the instance is a replaceable heap object; the standard notes that function-local static initialisation may be more efficient.
pitfalls: If the initialiser throws, the flag stays unset: guard against a permanently failing constructor being retried forever.
The flag and the instance need definitions in exactly one translation unit (or C++17 inline static members), or every including unit gets its own once_flag.
A heap instance is never destroyed by the accessor: add explicit teardown if the destructor matters.

variants.name: Pre-C++11 singleton (guarded accessor or platform once)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++11 the language supplied neither a memory model for data races nor a once-primitive, so the classic form had to lock on every access or delegate to a platform primitive (pthread_once, ACE_Singleton). The widespread double-checked locking shortcut was and remains unreliable, because the writes that construct the object and the store to the pointer may be reordered, or become visible out of order, on both uniprocessor and multiprocessor targets. Keep this variant only for toolchains that cannot move to C++11, and prefer the guarded accessor over DCLP there.
pitfalls: Double-checked locking is not portable here: volatile does not order the construction writes against the pointer store across threads (Meyers & Alexandrescu, 2004).
A heap instance leaks at exit, while a namespace-scope instance reintroduces the static-initialisation-order fiasco.
Each dynamic-library copy of the class gets its own instance on most platforms.
